cards.front: Adult human arterial plasma at rest holds about 24 mmol/L of bicarbonate and about {{c1::40 nanomoles}} of free hydrogen ions per litre.
cards.back: About 600,000-fold: about 24 millimolar against 40 nanomolar.
cards.quote: Adult human arterial plasma at rest holds about 24 millimoles of bicarbonate per litre and about 40 nanomoles of free hydrogen ions per litre.

cards.front: Human plasma pH is held near 7.40 on three clocks. Name the three defences and the time scale of each.
cards.back: Buffers in seconds, lungs in minutes, kidneys over days.
cards.quote: held on three clocks: buffers in seconds, lungs in minutes, kidneys over days.

cards.front: In human plasma, pH follows the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved CO2, which is {{c1::20 to 1}} at pH 7.40.
cards.quote: pH follows one ratio: bicarbonate over dissolved CO2, 20 to 1 at pH 7.40.

cards.front: Which organ sets each term of the bicarbonate / dissolved CO2 ratio in human plasma, and how fast does each act?
cards.back: The lungs set the bottom (CO2), starting within minutes. The kidney sets the top (bicarbonate), over days.
cards.quote: The lungs set the bottom of the ratio, starting within minutes; the kidney sets the top over days.

cards.front: In an acid-base disturbance, which way does compensation move the other term of the bicarbonate / CO2 ratio, and how far does it bring pH?
cards.back: In the same direction as the primary change, so the ratio moves back toward 20. Usually partway, sometimes nearly all the way in chronic respiratory disorders, never past 7.40.
cards.quote: Compensation moves the other term in the same direction, which brings the ratio back toward 20

cards.front: What is the difference between a volatile and a non-volatile acid in the body? Give examples of each.
cards.back: Volatile: CO2, which leaves as a gas through the lungs. Non-volatile: e.g. sulfuric acid from sulfur-containing amino acids, lactic acid, ketoacids; these are buffered, and the kidney excretes the net fixed-acid load.
cards.quote: A volatile acid leaves as a gas: carbon dioxide, removed by the lungs.

cards.front: A disturbance that starts with pCO2 is {{c1::respiratory}}; one that starts with non-volatile acid or base is metabolic.
cards.quote: A disturbance that starts with pCO2 is respiratory; one that starts with non-volatile acid or base is metabolic.

cards.front: Write the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for human plasma at 37 C, with its units.
cards.back: pH = 6.1 + log10([HCO3-] / (0.03 × pCO2)), with bicarbonate in mmol/L and pCO2 in mmHg; 0.03 × pCO2 is dissolved CO2 in mmol/L.

cards.front: Why is the 6.1 in the plasma Henderson-Hasselbalch equation not the pK of carbonic acid?
cards.back: It is an apparent pK that folds two steps together: hydration of CO2 and ionization to bicarbonate. Carbonic acid on its own is a much stronger acid.
cards.quote: Because the 6.1 folds hydration and ionization together, it is not the pK of carbonic acid

cards.front: A made-up sample of human plasma at 37 C has bicarbonate 48 mmol/L and pCO2 80 mmHg (both double the normal 24 and 40). What is its pH?
cards.back: Dissolved CO2 = 0.03 × 80 = 2.4 mmol/L; 48 / 2.4 = 20; pH = 6.1 + 1.30 = 7.40. Both terms doubled, so the ratio and pH are unchanged.
cards.why: pH follows the ratio, not either concentration.
cards.quote: Double both and pH does not move; change one alone and it does.

cards.front: A made-up sample of human plasma at 37 C has a normal bicarbonate of 24 mmol/L but pCO2 30 mmHg. What is its pH, and what does it show?
cards.back: Dissolved CO2 = 0.03 × 30 = 0.9 mmol/L; 24 / 0.9 = 26.7; pH = 6.1 + 1.43 = 7.53, an alkalemia. A normal bicarbonate does not mean a normal pH.
cards.quote: A normal bicarbonate does not mean a normal pH: the bottom of the fraction rose, so the ratio fell.

cards.front: The CO2/bicarbonate pair has a pK of 6.1, far below 7.40. Why would it be a poor buffer in a sealed bottle, yet it is the dominant extracellular buffer in the body?
cards.back: Sealed, each added proton turns bicarbonate into CO2, so the small CO2 term grows fast and pH crashes. In the body the lungs remove that CO2, so only the top of the ratio shrinks.
cards.why: At pH 7.40 only about one molecule in 21 of the pair is CO2.
cards.quote: In a sealed bottle, every proton you add turns a bicarbonate into CO2, so the small bottom of the ratio grows fast and pH crashes.
cards.section: Why this buffer works: it is open

cards.front: Made-up plasma with no other buffers (bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, pCO2 40 mmHg) receives 6 mmol/L of strong acid. Find pH if pCO2 is held at 40 mmHg (open) and if sealed in a syringe.
cards.back: Bicarbonate falls to 18. Open: dissolved CO2 stays 1.2; 18 / 1.2 = 15; pH = 6.1 + 1.18 = 7.28. Sealed: CO2 = 1.2 + 6 = 7.2; 18 / 7.2 = 2.5; pH = 6.1 + 0.40 = 6.50.
cards.quote: In the body the lungs remove that CO2, so the bottom of the ratio stays put and only the top shrinks.
cards.section: Why this buffer works: it is open

cards.front: Why does blood need carbonic anhydrase to unload CO2 in the lungs?
cards.back: Uncatalysed interconversion of CO2 and bicarbonate has a half-time of seconds to tens of seconds, but blood spends only about one second in a pulmonary capillary. The enzyme closes that gap.
cards.quote: Uncatalysed interconversion of CO2 and bicarbonate is slow, with a half-time of seconds to tens of seconds, while blood spends about one second in a pulmonary capillary
cards.section: Why this buffer works: it is open

cards.front: In a metabolic acidosis, when does respiratory compensation begin, and when does it reach its full steady-state extent?
cards.back: Breathing begins to deepen within minutes; the fall in pCO2 reaches its full extent over about 12 to 24 hours.
cards.quote: within minutes breathing begins to deepen and pCO2 falls too, reaching its full, steady-state extent over about 12 to 24 hours.
cards.section: Why this buffer works: it is open

cards.front: Where is an acute load of non-volatile acid buffered in the human body?
cards.back: In seconds, mainly by extracellular bicarbonate (to CO2 for the lungs), with plasma proteins and phosphate taking a smaller share, plus intracellular buffers. Over hours, cells and bone take a further share.
cards.why: H+ made from CO2 inside red cells is a different load, buffered mainly by hemoglobin.
cards.quote: Outside cells, bicarbonate takes up the protons and becomes CO2 for the lungs, with plasma proteins and phosphate taking a smaller share.
cards.section: Buffering is not removal: from seconds to days

cards.front: Why does buffering limit a pH change from a fixed-acid load without reversing it?
cards.back: Every proton a buffer holds is still in the body, and bicarbonate spent on the load is gone until the kidney makes more (or a retained lactate or ketoanion is metabolised).
cards.quote: Every proton a buffer holds is still in the body, and bicarbonate spent on a fixed-acid load is gone until the kidney makes more
cards.section: Buffering is not removal: from seconds to days

cards.front: What are the kidney's two acid-base jobs, and which one makes new base?
cards.back: Reclaiming filtered bicarbonate stops a loss but makes no new base. Making new bicarbonate by excreting acid is the only way to repay what the day's acid consumed.
cards.quote: Reclaiming filtered bicarbonate stops a loss but makes no new base; making new bicarbonate by excreting acid is the only way to repay what the day's acid consumed.

cards.front: Suppose a person filters 150 L a day at a plasma bicarbonate of 24 mmol/L, with a daily non-volatile acid load near 50 mEq. How much bicarbonate is filtered, and what would losing 2 percent of it cost?
cards.back: 150 × 24 = 3,600 mmol filtered a day. 2 percent is 72 mmol, more base than the day's ~50 mEq of acid consumes.
cards.why: Reclaiming must be nearly complete before new base can make any headway.
cards.quote: At 24 mmol/L, 165 L carries about 4,000 mmol of bicarbonate, roughly eighty times the day's non-volatile acid.

cards.front: Trace one filtered bicarbonate ion back to the blood across a mammalian proximal tubule cell.
cards.back: NHE3 and a V-type H+-ATPase secrete H+. Luminal carbonic anhydrase IV turns H+ + HCO3- into CO2 and water. CO2 enters the cell, carbonic anhydrase II rehydrates it, H+ is secreted again, and HCO3- exits basolaterally on NBCe1.
cards.why: One bicarbonate vanishes from the lumen and one appears in blood: no new base.
cards.quote: CO2 enters the cell, cytosolic carbonic anhydrase II rehydrates it, the H+ is secreted again, and the HCO3- leaves across the basolateral membrane

cards.front: A person takes acetazolamide, which blocks carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule. Predict urine bicarbonate, plasma bicarbonate and net acid excretion, and name the renal job that fails.
cards.back: Urine bicarbonate rises, plasma bicarbonate falls, and net acid excretion falls (its bicarbonate term grows). Reclaiming fails: base the body already had is lost.
cards.why: The indirect reclaiming route needs carbonic anhydrase; the glutamine-to-ammonium machinery is not the main target.
cards.quote: The indirect route needs carbonic anhydrase, so less filtered bicarbonate is reclaimed.

cards.front: A made-up day's urine is 2 L at pH 5.0. How many mmol of free H+ does it carry, and why must the kidney use buffers to excrete a ~50 mEq acid load?
cards.back: [H+] = 10^-5 mol/L; × 2 L = 2 × 10^-5 mol = 0.02 mmol. That is a tiny fraction of 50 mEq, so the acid must leave on buffers (phosphate, ammonium).
cards.quote: Urine pH bottoms out near 4.5, about 800 times plasma's free H+

cards.front: Net acid excretion = {{c1::titratable acid + NH4+ - HCO3-}}
cards.back: New bicarbonate is made in proportion to net acid excretion.
cards.quote: net acid excretion = titratable acid + NH4+ - HCO3-

cards.front: What is titratable acid, what normally sets its upper limit, and what share of net acid excretion is it?
cards.back: Protons carried on urinary buffers, mainly phosphate. Limited by how much phosphate reaches the urine. Normally about one-third to one-half of the total.
cards.quote: Titratable acid is protons carried on urinary buffers, mainly phosphate.

cards.front: Proximal tubule cells make two NH4+ and two HCO3- from each glutamine. Why does only ammonium excreted in urine count toward new bicarbonate?
cards.back: Ammonium returned to the blood is disposed of by the liver in a step that uses up the same bicarbonate, cancelling the gain.
cards.quote: If the ammonium goes back to the blood instead, the liver disposes of it in a step that uses up the same bicarbonate

cards.front: Under a sustained acid load, why does ammonium rather than titratable acid carry most of the rise in renal acid excretion?
cards.back: Titratable acid is capped by urinary phosphate, while ammonium production from glutamine can rise; so most of the extra acid leaves as ammonium.
cards.quote: titratable acid is capped by urinary phosphate, so most of the extra acid leaves as ammonium.

cards.front: A person in chronic metabolic acidosis has a urine pH of about 6. Does that show low renal ammonium excretion?
cards.back: No. In chronic acidosis ammonium excretion is high, yet urine pH can rise to about 6; urine pH is a poor index of ammonium excretion.
cards.quote: in chronic acidosis ammonium excretion is high and urine pH can rise to about 6, so urine pH is a poor index of ammonium excretion.

cards.front: Compare type-A and type-B intercalated cells of the mammalian collecting duct, membrane by membrane.
cards.back: Type-A: luminal V-type H+-ATPase, basolateral Cl-/HCO3- exchanger AE1; secretes acid, returns new HCO3- to blood. Type-B: the mirror, with luminal pendrin and basolateral H+-ATPase; secretes bicarbonate.
cards.quote: type-A intercalated cells pump H+ into the lumen through a V-type H+-ATPase and return the new HCO3- made inside the cell to the blood

cards.front: A made-up 24-hour urine contains 20 mEq titratable acid, 40 mEq ammonium and 2 mEq bicarbonate. Assuming all ammonium came from renal glutamine at 2 per glutamine, find net acid excretion and the glutamine used.
cards.back: NAE = 20 + 40 - 2 = 58 mEq/day. Glutamine = 40 / 2 = 20 mmol.
cards.quote: net acid excretion = titratable acid + NH4+ - HCO3-

cards.front: Textbook view: NH3 crosses membranes freely and is trapped as NH4+ in acid collecting-duct fluid. What did acid-loading Rhcg knockout mice show, and what does it imply?
cards.back: Knockouts could not acidify urine normally because ammonium excretion was impaired; their ducts had reduced apical NH3 permeability. Protein-mediated transport is required in the mouse collecting duct, contradicting the prediction that deletion would matter little.
cards.why: It does not show whether Rhcg carries NH3 or NH4+, or anything about humans.
cards.quote: The knockouts could not acidify urine normally because ammonium excretion was impaired

cards.front: A loss-of-function mutation hits the B1 subunit of the type-A cell's proton pump. Predict urine pH, net acid excretion, plasma bicarbonate and pCO2.
cards.back: Urine pH stays higher; net acid excretion falls (less titrated phosphate, less ammonium trapped); plasma bicarbonate and pH fall; ventilation rises so pCO2 falls (compensation).
cards.quote: Apical H+ pumping falls, so the duct builds a smaller gradient and urine pH stays higher.

cards.front: In acidosis from loss of the type-A proton pump B1 subunit, would you expect a raised or a normal anion gap? What happens to plasma chloride?
cards.back: Normal gap with raised chloride. No acid anion is added; bicarbonate is not replaced, and chloride takes its place.
cards.why: Rule: an added acid leaves its anion and raises the gap; lost or unreplaced bicarbonate is replaced by chloride.
cards.quote: The B1 pump failure above is this kind.

cards.front: In respiratory acidosis, how much does plasma bicarbonate rise per 10 mmHg rise in pCO2, acutely and over days?
cards.back: About 1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg at once (buffering) and about 5 per 10 mmHg over days (the kidney makes new bicarbonate).
cards.quote: Bicarbonate rises about 1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg at once, by buffering, and about 5 per 10 mmHg over days
cards.section: Compensation: the other organ pushes the same way

cards.front: pCO2 rises from 40 to 70 mmHg in a person whose bicarbonate was 24 mmol/L. Using about 1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg acutely and about 5 per 10 chronically, estimate bicarbonate and pH in each phase.
cards.why: Chronic renal compensation brings pH much nearer 7.40 but not past it.
cards.quote: about 5 per 10 mmHg over days as the kidney makes new bicarbonate
cards.section: Compensation: the other organ pushes the same way

cards.front: In a metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate 15 mmol/L, what pCO2 would fully restore pH 7.40, and what does Winter's formula predict?
cards.back: Full: pCO2 = 15 / (0.03 × 20) = 25 mmHg. Winter's: 1.5 × 15 + 8 = 30.5 ± 2 mmHg. Real compensation falls short of full.
cards.quote: In a metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate at 12 mmol/L, that means pCO2 = 12 / (0.03 × 20) = 20 mmHg.
cards.section: Compensation: the other organ pushes the same way

cards.front: In a blood gas, what does it mean if bicarbonate and pCO2 move in opposite directions, or compensation is far bigger or smaller than expected?
cards.back: Two disturbances are going on at once.
cards.why: A single disturbance plus compensation always moves both terms in the same direction.
cards.quote: So two numbers that move in opposite directions, or a compensation far bigger or smaller than expected, mean two things are going on at once.
cards.section: Compensation: the other organ pushes the same way

cards.front: Plasma pH is 7.10. What is [H+] in nmol/L, compared with normal?
cards.back: [H+] = 10^(9 - 7.10) ≈ 79 nmol/L, about twice the 40 nmol/L at pH 7.40.
cards.quote: [H+] = 10^-7.27 mol/L, which is 10^(9 - 7.27) = about 54 nmol/L, against 40 at pH 7.40.

cards.front: A made-up steady-state sample of human plasma has bicarbonate 16 mmol/L and pCO2 31 mmHg. Find pH, name the disorder, and check the compensation with Winter's formula.
cards.quote: expected pCO2 = 1.5 × bicarbonate + 8, plus or minus 2 mmHg.

cards.front: A patient with metabolic acidosis has bicarbonate 16 mmol/L but pCO2 22 mmHg. Compute pH and interpret against Winter's formula.
cards.back: 0.03 × 22 = 0.66; 16 / 0.66 = 24.2; pH ≈ 7.48. Expected pCO2 is 30 to 34; 22 is well below, so a second, respiratory alkalosis is added.
cards.why: Compensation never carries pH past 7.40, so an alkalemia here needs a second process.
cards.quote: A pCO2 well below 24 would mean the opposite, an added respiratory alkalosis.

cards.front: A sedated patient cannot raise ventilation and receives a fixed-acid load. Using the open-system principle, predict whether pH falls more or less than in an alert person, and why.
cards.back: More. CO2 made by buffering is not removed and ventilation cannot deepen, so the bottom of the ratio does not fall; the buffer approaches a closed one.
cards.why: Rule: the CO2/bicarbonate pair is powerful only because the lungs hold the CO2 term.
cards.quote: Being open is what makes it the dominant buffer of extracellular fluid.
cards.section: Why this buffer works: it is open

cards.front: A plasma bicarbonate of 30 mmol/L is reported with no pCO2. Can you call it a metabolic alkalosis?
cards.back: No. A primary rise in pCO2 also raises bicarbonate: about 1 per 10 mmHg by buffering, and about 5 per 10 over days by the kidney. You need pCO2 and pH to tell primary from compensation.
cards.quote: It is why plasma bicarbonate on its own mixes respiratory and metabolic effects.

cards.front: How does the anion gap separate the two kinds of metabolic acidosis?
cards.back: Gap = Na+ - Cl- - HCO3-. Acid added with an unmeasured anion (lactic, keto) uses up bicarbonate and leaves its anion: gap rises. Bicarbonate lost (gut or kidney) is replaced by chloride: gap stays normal.
cards.quote: Its H+ uses up bicarbonate and its anion stays behind, so the gap rises.

cards.front: A made-up sample has Na+ 138, Cl- 100, HCO3- 14 mmol/L and albumin 3.0 g/dL (normal 4.0). Compute the anion gap and the albumin-corrected gap.
cards.why: Albumin is the largest unmeasured anion, so low albumin hides part of a raised gap.
cards.quote: Corrected gap = 24 + 2.5 × (4.0 − 2.0) = 29 mmol/L

cards.front: A made-up sample has Na+ 140, Cl- 112 and HCO3- 16 mmol/L, against a normal gap of 12. What kind of metabolic acidosis fits?
cards.back: Gap = 140 - 112 - 16 = 12, normal; chloride rose as bicarbonate fell. Bicarbonate lost (gut or kidney) or not replaced, with chloride in its place.
cards.quote: Chloride takes its place, so plasma chloride rises and the gap stays normal.

cards.front: Winter's formula returns a pCO2 of 44 mmHg at a normal bicarbonate of 24. What does that tell you about compensation rules?
cards.back: They are regression lines fitted to observed people with real scatter, valid only for their disorder (Winter's: metabolic acidosis), not physical laws.
cards.quote: Winter's formula is a fit for metabolic acidosis only: at a normal bicarbonate of 24 it returns 44, not 40.

cards.front: A new drug lowers plasma bicarbonate. Design a human study to tell whether it impairs reclaiming filtered bicarbonate or making new bicarbonate, and give the separating results.
cards.back: Fixed diet, placebo period, timed urine (pH, HCO3-, titratable acid, NH4+) plus plasma, then an acid load. Reclaiming defect: bicarbonaturia, steep fractional excretion when plasma HCO3- is raised, normal NH4+ rise. New-base defect: low urine HCO3-, but NH4+ and titratable acid fail to rise.
cards.why: Check filtration is unchanged, since it alters every urinary number.
cards.quote: If it impairs making new bicarbonate, urine bicarbonate stays low, but ammonium and titratable acid fail to rise under the acid load

cards.front: People with Pendred syndrome lack pendrin. Why is their acid-base status normal at rest, yet they can develop severe metabolic alkalosis on thiazide-type diuretics?
cards.back: Pendrin lets type-B cells secrete bicarbonate, which matters most when an alkali load must be excreted. Without it, severe alkalosis developed on thiazide-type diuretics.
cards.quote: Their bicarbonate secretion matters most when the body must excrete an alkali load

cards.front: In the chicken, a leg vein drains into the peritubular region of the same-side kidney. What does infusing an agent into one leg buy over an intravenous infusion in a mammal, and what must still be measured?
cards.back: Each bird is its own control: systemic pH, pCO2, blood pressure and anaesthesia are shared. Flow, filtration, electrolytes and delivery on each side must still be measured, not assumed equal.
cards.quote: Each bird is its own control: systemic pH and pCO2, blood pressure and anaesthesia are shared
cards.section: An older experiment: one kidney as the other's control
